<reason>Both sides ran disciplined, well-shaped cases on an agreed metric (deaths by 2030), and both answered the pressure round in proper A1/A2 form. CON's best material was real: retention decay, the four-in-five coverage wall, the sharp 2024 inflection paired with record seizures, and the memorable "chain of voluntary steps / naloxone cannot be self-administered" reach argument, which exposed the weakest patch in PRO's answer to the solitary user. But PRO won the decisive clash. Its pressure question forced CON to abandon price transmission ("pressure cannot transmit through price"), and PRO correctly showed that price was load-bearing for CON's initiation-suppression and "users buy less" arguments — leaving CON with tonnage and indictments but no demonstrated scarcity. PRO's unfalsifiability framing ("if deaths rise the network is restructuring; if deaths fall the pressure caught up") landed cleanly and CON's closing repair only restated the concession rather than rebuilding the mechanism. That matters comparatively: CON's universality advantage is only worth what its mechanism delivers, and PRO showed the mechanism was unverified while conceding MAT's mortality benefit was granted as real. PRO also handled the retention attack well (the halving estimate already includes dropouts; the fix is lower-barrier care) and gave concrete, five-year-feasible regulatory levers. CON's late "spot shortages in several western markets" was slightly brittle. Competitive, but PRO made the choice easier to resolve.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's pressure question on the missing price/purity signal, and its exploitation of CON's answer ("pressure cannot transmit through price"), which gutted CON's initiation-suppression and reduced-consumption arguments and reframed enforcement as activity rather than scarcity.</best_rebuttal>
